opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core issue is that when you train on internet data, you're fundamentally learning to imitate the distribution of what people have written down. And that's incredibly powerful. It gets you language, it gets you a lot of world knowledge, it gets you reasoning patterns that humans have expressed. But imitation has a natural limit: at best, you converge toward something like the average, or maybe the best, of what's in that distribution. You're not going to systematically exceed it just by predicting the next token more accurately.

And if you think about the hardest problems, the frontier of mathematics, for example, by definition the answers aren't on the internet. Nobody has written down the proof of a theorem that hasn't been proven yet. So if your only training signal is "match what humans wrote," you don't have a mechanism for going beyond human knowledge. You've kind of capped yourself at the level of the data.

There's also a quality problem. The internet is full of reasoning that looks plausible but is subtly wrong. A lot of math on the internet has errors, gaps, hand-waving. If you train on that, the model learns to produce things that sound right, which is not the same as things that are right. And for a field like math, where correctness is binary, that distinction matters enormously.

So the way we think about it is that to break through that ceiling, you need a different kind of signal, something that tells you whether you're actually correct rather than whether you sound like a human. That's why we're so focused on formal verification. In a system like Lean, a proof either checks or it doesn't. That gives you a ground-truth reward you can use for reinforcement learning, and it lets the model generate its own data, try things, fail, learn, and eventually discover things nobody has written down. That's the same dynamic that let AlphaGo surpass human play: it wasn't limited to imitating human games once it could play against itself with a clear win condition.

So internet data is a great starting point. It's a bootstrap. But if you want superhuman reasoning, you need a training loop grounded in verifiable truth, not just human text.

r001.rationale: The response says internet-text imitation has a ceiling at the level of the data and notes that plausible but incorrect online reasoning limits what models learn.

r002.rationale: It describes generating data and learning from attempts, and compares this to AlphaGo self-play, but does not claim self-play is necessary to surpass mathematicians and researchers across multiple tasks.

r003.rationale: It says the model can try, fail, and learn, but does not state that generated training data should become more complex as the model improves.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that internet data is a record of what humans have already figured out and bothered to write down. When you train on it, you're essentially compressing the existing frontier of human knowledge into a model. That's incredibly powerful, and it gets you something that can recall, synthesize, and remix everything we've collectively produced. But by construction, it can't get you past that frontier, because the things that lie beyond it haven't been written down by anyone yet.

There's a second problem, which is that most of the data on the internet is the output of reasoning, not the reasoning itself. A math paper shows you the polished proof, not the ten failed attempts, the wrong turns, the moment where the author realized the lemma they needed didn't hold. So the model learns what correct answers look like, but it gets a very thin signal about how to actually search for them. And when you push these models into genuinely novel territory, where pattern-matching to something seen before doesn't work, that gap shows up immediately.

The third piece is that internet text has no built-in notion of truth. The model is learning the distribution of what people say, and people are wrong a lot. In most domains there's no cheap way to check, so you can't easily filter for correctness, and you certainly can't generate an unlimited amount of new, verified data. You're stuck with a fixed, noisy corpus that we're already close to exhausting.

That's why I'm so drawn to domains like mathematics, where you have a formal verifier. Once you can mechanically check whether an output is correct, the data ceiling disappears. The model can attempt problems, get a perfect reward signal, and generate its own training data indefinitely. You move from imitating humans to actually discovering things, and that's a fundamentally different regime than scaling up on more web text.

r001.rationale: The response says internet data compresses existing human knowledge and that models cannot get past that frontier because beyond-frontier knowledge has not been written down.

r002.rationale: It describes generating training data through attempts with formal verification, but does not say self-play is necessary to surpass human mathematicians and researchers across multiple tasks.

r003.rationale: It says models can generate training data indefinitely, but does not describe increasing problem complexity as models improve iteratively.

astra-6.text:
I think the internet is a record of what people have chosen to write down, and that’s only a fraction of what people know how to do. You can read a lot about programming, for example, without seeing all the failed attempts, the debugging, and the feedback that led to the final piece of code.

So if you train only on that record, you eventually run into a limit on what you can learn from it. That doesn’t mean a model can’t generalize or discover something new. But to keep improving, it needs a way to try things and find out whether they work—to write a program and execute it, or make a prediction and test it.

The important distinction is between learning from descriptions of the world and learning from interacting with the world. Internet data gives you a powerful starting point. It doesn’t give you an unlimited source of feedback.

r001.rationale: The response says internet data is only a partial record of what people know and do, so training only on it eventually limits what a model can learn.

r002.rationale: It calls for models to try things and test results, but does not present self-play as necessary to surpass human mathematicians and researchers across multiple tasks.

r003.rationale: It does not propose using model-generated training data or increasing that data's complexity as models improve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the internet is a record of what people chose to write down, and that’s a much smaller set than everything people know how to do. You can read a lot about programming, for example, but the finished code doesn’t necessarily show you all the failed attempts, the feedback, and the decisions that led to it.

So training on internet data gives you an incredibly powerful starting point. But if that’s your only source of learning, you’re constrained by what’s already been documented. To go beyond that, a model needs to try things, observe the consequences, and learn from feedback. In programming, that could mean writing code, running it, seeing what breaks, and fixing it. That gives you a source of experience that isn’t limited to the text people have put online.

r001.rationale: The response says internet data limits learning to what has been documented, but does not identify the quality of that data as a ceiling on attainable intelligence.

r002.rationale: It describes models trying tasks and learning from feedback, but does not present self-reinforcing self-play as necessary to surpass human mathematicians and researchers across multiple tasks.

r003.rationale: It mentions learning through attempts and feedback, but does not propose increasing the complexity of model-generated training data as models improve.
